relations.note: Agassou appears as Agwe's ancestral-houngan lieutenant, represented by a crab.
Ayida gives Agassou a crab for his transatlantic voyage.
Modern narratives say Ayida selected Agassou to carry Vodou across the Atlantic.
House-dependent catalogues place Agassou within Dambala's suite.
A Haitian song places Agassou and Loko together in the mirror.
Recent regional summaries allege that Ayida deceives Danbala through a liaison with the sea lwa Agwe.

relations.myth: Ayida becomes Agwe’s lover at sea
relations.note: Ayida becomes Agwe’s lover, and Damballa knows that she is unfaithful.
Freda is Agwe's wife, joining cultivated love with maritime wealth and water.
Gu is Agbé's younger sibling or another later child of Mawu-Lisa.
La Sirène is Agwe's wife, consort, and co-ruler of the waters.
Agwe and La Sirène inhabit a splendid palace beneath or beyond the sea.
Agwe and La Sirène are jointly honored and represented in sacred art.
relations.source: André Pierre, Ceremony for Agoue and La Sirene

relations.note: His ceremony praises La Sirène and sends offerings to their underwater realm.
Agwe and Loko depart Ayizan's household and assume separate domains.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Mawu-Lisa produces Agbé and assigns him the sea and its life.
relations.source: Herskovits and Herskovits, Outline; Herskovits, Dahomey

relations.note: Agwe's acceptance or refusal of an offshore offering is interpreted within the wider spirit community.
Agwe shares Simbi’s aquatic domain but is maritime rather than freshwater-local.
A funeral song sends the dead to Sobo and Bade, then to Agwe's house.
Sogbo and Agbé are siblings heading the sky and sea domains.
Bossou offers a bowl of blood rather than wine at Ayida Wedo's wedding.
Haitian tradition identifies Ayida as Danbala Wedo’s wife and rainbow counterpart.
Modern retellings say Danbala sees the newly appeared rainbow Ayida, loves her, and marries her.
Ayida and Danbala are complementary female and male aspects of one cosmic serpent principle.
Some lineages regard Ayida and Damballa as female and male aspects of one mystery.
Danbala crosses beneath or across the sea while Ayida travels above as a rainbow; they reunite in Haiti.

relations.myth: Intertwined serpents generate or renew life
relations.note: Their intertwined union represents fertility, balance, and the renewal of life.
Danbala and Ayida are paired as husband and wife in many Haitian traditions.
Some traditions treat Danbala and Ayida as dual aspects of one serpent principle.
Ouidah traditions and scholarship associate or derive Dan Aido-Hwedo from Dangbé while distinguishing their characteristic forms.
Some modern traditions call Ayida Freda's rival because both are linked to Danbala.
Aido-Hwedo carries the creator while its winding motion shapes the world.
At the creator’s command, Aido-Hwedo coils beneath the earth and supports it above the sea.
Ayida is indirectly associated with Simbi through shared aquatic-serpentine symbolism.

relations.myth: The first mambo and first oungan
relations.note: Ayizan and Loko jointly guard initiation, temples, ritual knowledge, and priestly transmission.
They jointly protect initiation, ritual purity, and priestly transmission.
relations.source: Marcelin, Métraux, and later Haitian ethnography

relations.note: Later Haitian theology often presents the priestly pair as husband and wife.
Loko lived in Ayizan's house, revolted, and departed to assume a separate domain.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.myth: Legba, Loko, and Ayizan walk together
relations.note: A regional liturgy places Loko before Ayizan and says they walk with Legba.
Modern comparativists occasionally propose Ayizan as Brigitte’s Fon equivalent.
Some ritual summaries place the Marassa after Ayizan rather than Legba.
An Agasu priest's oral tradition claims Ayizan preceded Sagbata's arrival.
Deren contrasts Azaka’s insecure appetite and comic sexuality with Gede’s deliberate transgression.
Gede attends Azaka’s ceremony, protects and indulges him, and exploits the dependable feast.
Deren reports that Gede and Azaka are considered brothers.
Some Haitian compilations call agricultural Zaka a cousin of Ogou Feray.
Loko appears briefly and is saluted during Azaka’s service.
Zaka and Loko depart Ayizan's household during the same divine exodus.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Ogou Feray and Zaka are frequently called cousins or companions.
Ritual drama places Ogou with Zaka when Zaka is accused of theft.
Legba is invoked to open the gate before Azaka is called.
Contemporary teaching says Azaka works with Sobo’s rain and thunder power to make earth productive.
Baron stands beneath the supreme creator Bondye in Vodou theology.
Gede may refuse to bury someone whom Bawon has unjustly marked for death.
relations.source: Herskovits, Life in a Haitian Valley

relations.note: Deren repeatedly presents Baron Samedi and Gede as alternative identities.
Later teachings make Bawon father or king of the innumerable Gede.
Some traditions place Bawon as ruler or principal figure of the Gede.
Baron and Carrefour jointly govern invisible forces employed in dangerous magic.
Deren structurally interprets Baron as brother to Carrefour.
Baron and Brijit jointly govern the cemetery and death complex.

relations.myth: Brigitte and Bawon rule the cemetery
relations.note: They jointly govern cemeteries and passage between life and death.
She is Baron's wife, female cemetery counterpart, and co-ruler of the dead.
Deren associates Baron and Simbi with magical operations and protective pakèt.
Damballa remains subordinate to the remote creator in Haitian theological structure.
Freda serves beneath the remote creator within the lwa-mediated Vodou cosmos.
Gede remains subordinate to Bondye and cannot reverse a death God has fixed.
Some accounts call the Marasa Bondye’s earliest creations or first children.
An alternative formulation calls the Marassa Bondye’s first creation.
Lineage-specific formulations metaphorically describe the Marasa as Bondye’s first children.
The Marassa are described as Bondye’s first children, closest to the divine source.
Haitian comparison links both as remote creators, without establishing lexical identity.
Legba mediates ritual access within a cosmos ultimately governed by Bondye.
Bossou offers a bowl of blood rather than wine at Damballah's wedding.
Kalfou and Bosou are both served by reported Makaya, Bizango, and Sanpwel groups.
A disputed reconstruction presents Bossou as another name or manifestation of Sakpata.
Scholars connect Damballa historically with Whydah’s royal python vodun without asserting literal identity.

relations.myth: Cool serpent contrasted with heated warrior
relations.note: Deren contrasts Damballah's cool antiquity with Ogou's heated warrior temperament.

relations.myth: Aido-Hwedo assists the creator forming the world
relations.note: As Aido-Hwedo, the serpent carries or assists Mawu-Lisa during creation.
After creation, the serpent coils beneath the earth or establishes supports stabilizing it.
Deren interprets Ti Jean's footless tree-climbing as analogous to Danbala's serpent nature.
Some Haitian lineages describe Erzulie Freda as Damballah's lover or concubine.
Gu, Legba and Dan are invoked together to animate protective objects.
Ayido-Hwedo transports Mawu-Lisa during creation and later supports the completed earth.

relations.myth: Dantò and Freda contend over Ogou
relations.note: Dantò is Ogou’s lover or partner; traditions variously specify Feray, Badagri, Chango, or another Ogou.
Some houses treat Ti Jean as Dantò’s closely allied ritual companion.
A documented praise-song calls Dantò Ti Jean’s woman; some traditions call him her husband or lover.
Some oral genealogies identify Ti Jean as Dantò’s son or the child she carries.
Some modern accounts name Gede among Freda's lovers.
Modern discourse contrasts Freda's refined eroticism with Gede's disruptive sexuality.
Some traditions conflate them because both embody beauty, wealth, and aquatic associations.
Some lineages describe the affiliated watery and beautiful Lasirèn as Freda's sister.
Ogou is Freda's husband or impassioned lover, with identity varying by lineage.
Deren links Grand Bois, Carrefour, and Ghede in an underworld movement.

relations.myth: Governance of magic and the dead
relations.note: Gede governs dealings with the dead while Kalfou governs dangerous nocturnal passage.
Later traditions call Brigitte mother and senior female authority of the Gede.
Some Gede songs and rites invoke the Marasa alongside the dead.
Gede possesses someone prematurely, refuses to leave, and demands his attributes.
Contemporary houses say they collaborate in magic or secret-society work.
Deren places Grand Bois near Carrefour within her underworld cosmology.

relations.myth: Masters of woods, crossroads, and cemetery
relations.note: A song places Gran Bwa in woods and Mèt Kafou at crossroads.
At midnight Kalfou and Gran Bwa jointly govern magical practice with Baron Cimetière.
Other houses distinguish the spirits but say Gran Bwa and Loko walk together.
Rigaud associates the ritual post with both Papa Loko and Maître Grand Bois.
Some houses understand Gran Bwa as Loko’s Petwo road or manifestation.
Gu is described as Mawu-Lisa's divine child or agent.

relations.myth: Gu clears and equips the world
relations.note: Mawu-Lisa creates or dispatches Gu to clear and organize creation.
Mawu-Lisa equips and commissions Gu to finish the world's material work.
Ogou is historically related to the Fon iron divinity through Atlantic transmission and Haitian transformation.

relations.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
relations.note: Legba communicates between the iron and war vodun and Mawu.
Pantheon genealogies commonly list the iron and war vodun among Legba’s siblings.
Gu appears with Sakpata among associated earthly divinities.
Mawu-Lisa creates Hevioso or Sogbo and assigns him sky and thunder.
Abomey systematizations describe the thunder deity as Mawu-Lisa's child.
Some systematizations subordinate the thunder department to Mawu-Lisa.

relations.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
relations.note: Legba translates messages because Hevioso no longer speaks Mawu’s language.
Pantheon genealogies commonly list the thunder deity among Legba’s siblings.
The thunder and earth powers quarrel after Mawu apportions their respective domains.
Their quarrel leaves Xevioso ruling the sky and Sakpata the earth.
In complementary accounts, Hevioso sends rain to the earth governed by Sakpata.
Sakpata and the thunder power are described as brothers.
Sobo’s thunder and lightning operate jointly with Badé’s wind in Haitian service.
Some regional traditions make the generative Sogbo Hevioso’s mother or progenitor.
Rigaud identifies or associates Sobo with Québiésou, the Dahomean thunder power Hevioso.
Dahomean compilations describe Gbade as Sogbo’s youngest and unruly child.
Haitian traditions commonly describe Sobo and wind-governing Badé as brother lwa.
Métraux classifies Maître Carrefour as Legba-Petwo, the magically potent Petwo manifestation of Legba.

relations.myth: The two powers at the gate
relations.note: Kalfou sits opposite Legba, dividing nocturnal intercardinal forces from Legba’s daylight cardinal authority.
Simbi sometimes joins Kalfou, Gede, and Gran Bwa in governing forces required for magic.

relations.myth: Agwe and Ogoun feud over Ezili
relations.note: La Sirène’s overlap with Ezili implicates her in Agwe and Ogoun’s rivalry.
Loko is classified as a later child or member of the Mawu-Lisa pantheon.
Loko joins the departing group for which Sobo makes a signal flag.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Modern interpreters propose that Mawu-Lisa's duality is reflected by Haitian divine twins.
Scholars compare their complementary duality, without securely identifying the Marassa as Mawu and Lisa.
Legba opens the road, after which the Marassa are normally saluted.
Around Léogâne and in some rites, the Marassa receive precedence over Legba.
The paired creator is also presented as Legba’s parent.
Mawu-Lisa assigns Nyohwe Ananu authority within the earth pantheon.
Mawu-Lisa produces Nyohwe Ananu within the paired earth complex.
In Dahomean cosmology, Mawu-Lisa generates Sogbo and assigns him the sky.
Mawu-Lisa grants Sogbo authority over sky, thunder, or atmosphere.
Mawu-Lisa produces Sogbo among the departmental divine children.

relations.myth: Papa Lébat opens access to Louisiana spirits
relations.note: Later recollections portray him as the doorkeeper mediating ritual access to other Louisiana spirits.
Sobo announces himself during Ogou's absence and claims responsibility for Ogou's dog biting someone.

relations.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
relations.note: Legba observes Sagbata’s rule and carries communications between Sagbata and Mawu.
Pantheon genealogies commonly list the earth deity among Legba’s siblings.
Sogbo governs sky while his cosmological sibling Sakpata governs earth.
Deren structurally links Simbi between the Dan–Ti Jean Petro and Danbala complexes.
Modern sources name him alongside Simbi Makaya as Ezili Dantò’s husbands.

Aflado.note: Aflado, equated regionally with Agasu, appears within the Sakpata family list.

Agaou.note: One modern commentary says Agaou reigns jointly with Agwe.

Agawou.note: Weakly sourced modern lists claim Sobo and Bade jointly call Agawou and produce a thunderstorm.

Agbe.note: Herskovits-derived classifications make Agbe one of Sogbo’s children governing the sea.
Another genealogy makes Agbe and Hevioso separate children of Mawu-Lisa.
Mawu-Lisa produces Agbe as one of the paired water deities.
Mawu-Lisa assigns Agbe jurisdiction over the sea and waters.
Pantheon genealogies commonly list Agbe among Legba’s siblings.

Agbe.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
Agbe.note: Legba connects Agbe’s sea domain with Mawu through translation.
Sogbo and Agbe hold distinct sibling jurisdictions over sky and sea.

Age.note: Gu and Age appear as Mawu-Lisa's children with divided cosmic occupations.
Mawu-Lisa produces Age among the departmental divine children.
Mawu-Lisa grants Age the bush, wild animals, and hunting.
Pantheon genealogies commonly list Age among Legba’s siblings.

Age.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
Age.note: Legba connects Age’s hunter, forest, or agricultural domain with Mawu.

Aido-Hwedo.note: Damballa is frequently equated with Dahomey’s cosmic serpent, though the dossier treats them as historically distinct.

Aido-Hwedo.myth: Formation and support of the earth
Aido-Hwedo.note: The cosmic serpent carries Mawu while its movements shape the terrain.

Aido-Hwedo.myth: Formation and support of the earth
Aido-Hwedo.note: Mawu creates the surrounding sea to cool the world-supporting serpent.
At Mawu's command, Aido-Hwedo coils beneath or around the earth.

Ajahuto.note: Some traditions make Ajahuto Agasu's son or a more remote descendant.
Some modern retellings collapse Ajahuto into Agasu.

Aklombé.note: Later pantheon lists identify Aklombé as a child of Hevioso or Sogbo.

Aldkpe.note: This water spirit is associated with Da within the Sakpata complex.

Aligbonon.note: Aligbonon bears Agasu after union with a leopard-being.
Aligbonon.source: Le Hérissé, L’ancien royaume du Dahomey

Aligbonon.note: A rare account makes Agasu and his mother parents together.

Anaïs.note: Some lineages name Anaïs as Dantò’s daughter and identify her as the child in Dantò’s icon.

Asaka.note: The musical transforms Azaka into Asaka, a female earth deity.

Asojano.note: Arará traditions preserve this diasporic form linked with the Gbe Sakpata complex.

Avlekete.note: Some Mahi and coastal traditions describe Avlekete as Hevioso’s wife.
Other classifications make Avlekete a child within Hevioso’s thunder-sea family.

Awe.note: Mawu invites or orders Monkey to assist by preparing and shaping clay.
Monkey claims he can rival Mawu but cannot give life to clay bodies.
Mawu condemns Monkey to remain an animal after exposing his creative incapacity.
In an expanded version, Lisa gives Monkey porridge containing death.

Baron Cimetière.note: Early catalogue traditions describe him as Baron's brother.
Later systems sometimes treat Cimetière as an aspect of Samedi.
Deren places Cimetière among Baron forms governing magical operations.
Kalfou and Baron Cimetière join Gran Bwa in the midnight triad patronizing magicians.

Baron Kriminel.note: Some popular systems present Kriminel as a form of Samedi.

Baron La Croix.note: Early catalogue traditions describe the Barons as brothers.
Later systems sometimes treat La Croix as an aspect of Samedi.
They share authority within the cemetery and Gede ritual field.

Baron Maître Cimetière.note: Maître Carrefour and Baron Maître Cimetière appear together in secret-society ceremonial accounts.

Baron Piquant.note: Catalogue material calls this harsh grave-working Baron Samedi's brother.

Bawon Kriminèl.note: He participates in the Gede complex, sometimes as a distinct allied cemetery lwa.

Bawon Lakwa.myth: Masters of woods, crossroads, and cemetery
Bawon Lakwa.note: A song juxtaposes Gran Bwa in the woods with Bawon Lakwa in the cemetery.

Bawon Simityè.note: Later systems group Gran Bwa, Kalfou, and Bawon Simityè as forest, roads, and death.

Bazou.note: A speculative Kongo comparison equates Bossou with the high spirit Bazou.

Bosikpon.note: Oral testimony says Agasu was installed in Bosikpon's pre-existing leopard temple.
Bosikpon.source: Blier, The Path of the Leopard

Bosu.note: This female vodun guards Sakpata's divine household and orders its ceremonies.

Boukman’s invoked deity.myth: Later identification of Dantò at Bois Caïman
Boukman’s invoked deity.note: Modern national tradition identifies Dantò with the power invoked at Bois Caïman, though early accounts do not.

Chanprèl.note: Chanprèl and Ti Jean are jointly invoked to light the fire.

Christian God.note: Haitian practice often directly identifies Bondye with the Christian God.

Congo Savanne.note: Deren groups Ti Jean with Congo Savanne among major Petwo powers.

Congo Zandor.note: Later classifications identify Ti Jean as Ti Jean Zandor or associate him with Zandor.

Da Ayido Hwedo.note: The Sakpata-family member Dji is identified with Da Ayido Hwedo.

Da Langan.note: Da Langan is classified as another senior son in the Sakpata family.
An alternative ritual classification describes Da Langan as Sakpata's sibling.

Da Tokpo.note: Da Tokpo governs the Sakpata family in Da Zodji's place.

Da Zodji.note: Mawu-Lisa produces Da Zodji, a member of the earth complex.
Mawu-Lisa assigns Da Zodji authority over earth and its riches.
Da Zodji is classified as Sakpata's senior son.
He exercises authority over the Sakpata family in the aged father's place.

Dakodonu.note: A minority genealogy names Dakodonu as Agasu and Aligbonon's child.

Dan Petro.note: Deren calls Ti Jean the son of Dan Petro.

Danbala.note: Danbala is saluted among the senior spirits during Azaka’s service.
Some later interpretations call Danbala Bondye’s first creation or eldest servant.

Danbala Laflanbo.note: Kalfou and Danbala Laflanbo are both served by reported Makaya, Bizango, and Sanpwel groups.

Danbala Wedo.note: Loko and Danbala Wedo are greeted together in an initiation sequence.
Danbala and Loko join the divine exodus from Ayizan's household.
Danbala Wedo.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

Danbala Wèdo.note: Freda is his wife, and one of her three rings represents their marriage.
Simbi and Danbala share serpent and aquatic symbolism and ritual juxtaposition.

Death.note: Segbo sends Hevioso to steal or recover Death’s sickle, but Hevioso survives.

Djo.note: Mawu-Lisa produces Djo among the departmental divine children.
Mawu-Lisa assigns Djo authority over air or atmosphere.
Pantheon genealogies commonly list Djo among Legba’s siblings.

Djo.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
Djo.note: Djo receives humanity’s language while Legba retains knowledge of every language.

Don Petwo.note: Later traditions call him founder, ancestor, leader, or eponym of the Petwo lwa.

Dosa.note: The girl born after twins completes the Marassa pair as a powerful third term.

Dosou.note: The boy born after twins completes and concentrates their force, sometimes surpassing them.

Erzulie.note: Ogou and Erzulie enact desire, jealousy, betrayal and gendered social conflict.

Eve.note: A modern synthesis symbolically associates Brigitte and Bawon with Eve and Adam.

Ezili.note: Ezili is saluted among the key spirits during Azaka’s service.
Local traditions juxtapose or erotically link a Gede with an Ezili.
A ritual song names Ezili as Sobo's most beautiful woman and mistress.

Ezili Dantor.note: Some Dantor lineages call Ti Jean Dantor her son or only child.
Other traditions alternatively make Ti Jean her lover or husband.

Ezili Dantò.note: Kalfou and Ezili Dantò are both served by reported Makaya, Bizango, and Sanpwel groups.
Some traditions describe Dantò as Ogou’s partner or fierce counterpart.
Dantò and Freda fight over Ogou, and Dantò receives facial scars.
Some modern traditions call Simbi Makaya the husband of Ezili Dantò.

Ezili Freda.note: Some accounts make Ezili Freda Damballa’s wife, lover, or concubine.
Deren presents La Sirène as resembling or partly overlapping with marine Ezili.
Ezili Freda and Loko depart Ayizan's household during the same revolt.
Ezili Freda.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

Ezili Freda.note: Freda is frequently described as Ogou’s wife or lover.
Ezili Freda.source: Deren, Divine Horsemen; Brown, Mama Lola

Fa.note: Fa divination reveals Gu's needs, dispositions and required sacrifices.
Thunder priests consult Fa to determine a strike’s cause and required ritual settlement.
Mawu-Lisa commissions or authorizes Fa's divinatory order in differing accounts.
Legba guards Fa’s threshold and enables sacrificial responses to divined destiny.
Fa reveals destiny while Legba mediates the sacrifice that may change it.

Faith, Hope, and Charity.note: The three female Catholic personifications serve as a visual image of Marassa Twa.

Fon Lɛgbà.note: The Haitian Kalfou complex is reconstructed as a differentiation within the older Fon Legba crossroads tradition.

Ganyehesu.note: A minority genealogy names Ganyehesu as Agasu and Aligbonon's child.

Gaya-Dantò.note: A recent online ritual places Dantò’s protection over a feast for Zaka.

Gbadu.note: Mawu-Lisa authorizes the order through which Gbadu transmits Fa knowledge.

Gede Doub.note: Doub walks with the collective as a Gede associated with second sight.

Gede Linto.note: Linto shares rites with the collective as a locally attested Gede.

Gede Loray.note: Loray shares rites with the collective as the locally attested Gede Thunder.

Gede Mazaka.note: The compound name suggests overlap between the Gede and Azaka spirit complexes.
Mazaka walks with the collective as a locally variable Gede family member.

Gede Nibo.note: Later systems call him the son of Baron and Brijit.
Some Herskovits-era sources identify Baron Samedi with Gede Nimbo.
Nibo is described as a child, lieutenant, or major manifestation within the Gede family.
Gede Nibo.source: Deren, Métraux, oral narratives and songs

Gede Nibo.note: The Gede family receives Nibo after his premature or violent death.
Gede Nibo sometimes claims to be Brigitte’s child.

Gede Oussou.note: Oussou shares rites with the family, though spellings may represent separate identities.

Gede Ti Malis.note: Gede Ti Malis participates as a local family member bearing the trickster’s name.

Gede spirits.note: Some systems make Baron the father or patriarch of the Gede.
Some systems describe the Gede as Baron's subjects or family.
Some houses treat the Gede as manifestations of Baron.

Gran Ibo.note: Modern teachings distinguish Gran Bwa’s forest from Gran Ibo’s swamp and plant wisdom.

Gran Mèt.note: Rigaud makes Sobo a celestial escort of the supreme master.
Rigaud likewise makes Bade a celestial escort of the supreme master.

Gran Èzili.note: The elder Èzili praises Freda, whom Deren treats as a distinct spirit.

Grand Bois.note: Deren names Grand Bois with Baron among authorities over dangerous magic.

Grann Brijit.note: Later teachings call Brijit mother or queen of the Gede.

Guede Roussou Mazaca.note: Rigaud describes Sobo as an intermediary of this Guede figure.

Gun.note: Some modern Beninese summaries call the iron vodun Gun Hevioso’s twin.

Huntin.note: Huntin and Loko are jointly invoked as agencies for causing another's death.

Jean Petwo.note: Modern spirit lists distinguish Jean Petwo from Ti Jean and identify him as Dantò’s spouse or lover.

Jean-Jacques Dessalines.note: The assassinated emperor becomes, incarnates or joins the Ogou spirit family.
Jean-Jacques Dessalines.source: Paul, Dayan, Thornton and oral tradition

Jean-Jacques Dessalines.note: Posthumous tradition transforms Dessalines into a lwa or form of Ogou.

Jesus Christ.note: Christian-Vodou discourse variably presents Jesus as Bondye’s divine Son and savior.

Kabwatye.note: Modern online lists claim Kabwatye is the child of Bossou and Madan Bossou.

Konikoni.note: Mawu gives Konikoni to Legba as his wife.

Kouzinn.note: Some lineage teaching presents Kouzinn and Azaka as a farming husband and market-trading wife.
Kouzinn.source: Brown, Mama Lola; Florida teaching material

Kouzinn.note: Azaka’s female market counterpart handles or mediates collection of money he has lent.

Kpo.note: Agasu was assimilated to the male leopard and Kpo cult.

Kuxòsu.note: Kuxòsu is classified as father and oldest member of the Sakpata family.

La Baleine.myth: La Sirène and La Baleine song
La Baleine.note: They are jointly invoked as companions within the underwater spirit complex.

Lasirèn.note: Lasirèn and Dantò are classified together as distinct female sacred possibilities within the Èzili complex.

Lazarus.note: The beggar’s age, sores, staff, and dogs correspond to old Legba.

Legba.myth: Ayizan follows Legba in ceremonial order
Legba.note: Ayizan follows Legba ceremonially; both guard markets, roads, gates, doors, and barriers.
Some Haitian traditions call Ayizan Legba's wife or female counterpart.
Legba opens access to lwa; Baron or Gede opens access to the dead.
Some songs and modern analyses count Legba among Freda's lovers.
Legba must open ritual communication before Gede can arrive.
Deren interprets Gede as Legba transformed through passage into death.

Legba.myth: Legba’s descending world-tree aspect bears the name Grand Bois
Legba.note: Deren presents Grand Bois as Legba’s western, arboreal, underworld transformation.
Gu and Legba jointly animate protective or aggressive magical objects.

Legba.myth: Legba opens access before Ogou's salutation
Legba.note: Legba ritually opens access before Ogou and other lwa are saluted.
A Rara performance salutes Legba and then Papa Loko.

Legba.myth: Ayizan walks with Legba and Loko
Legba.note: Marcelin places Legba and Loko together as companions of Ayizan.
Legba is Mawu-Lisa's youngest and favored divine child.
Mawu-Lisa gives Legba all divine languages and appoints him mediator.

Legba.myth: Legba opens the gate for the other lwa
Legba.note: Legba enables ritual communication with the collective and is invoked before its members arrive.
Legba ritually precedes access to Simbi and other lwa.

Lemba.note: A speculative reconstruction transfers Bazou's fatherhood of Lemba into the proposed Bossou complex.

Li Grand Zombi.note: Some scholars equate Louisiana’s serpent spirit with Damballa, but historical identity remains unproven.
Later Louisiana interpretation associates the sacred-serpent title with Danbala, though historical equivalence remains unproved.

Lisa.note: Divided-gender accounts enumerate Gu among Lisa's children.
In the Segbo narrative, Lisa is Hevioso’s maternal grandfather.
Lisa assists Hevioso and his mother through Segbo’s attempts to destroy them.
Lisa is the male, solar component or aspect of the compound creator.
Mawu and Lisa are described as divine twins.
Mawu and Lisa unite as spouses or sexual complements and generate gods.

Lègba.note: Lègba serves as messenger and receives the first share of Sakpata sacrifices.

Madan Bossou.note: Certain contemporary lists describe Madan Bossou as Bossou's wife or feminine counterpart.

Maho.note: Maho, renamed Gbemende by Lisa, gives birth to Hevioso.
His mother restrains or mediates Hevioso’s continuing fury against Segbo.

Makandal.myth: Bossou restrains the dangerous deified Makandal
Makandal.note: Bossou is said to bind or restrain the deified Makandal.
Makandal.source: Modern Petwo synthesis and oral lore

Mami Wata.note: Louisiana occult writing links Agassou's crab emblem with Mami Wata.
Modern comparative systems equate Agwe with Mami Wata without historical proof.
Modern discourse identifies or compares La Sirène with the trans-African water-spirit complex.
Online sources occasionally assert Mami Wata as an African form of Brigitte.
Mami Wata is frequently present alongside Sakpata in Ouidah temples.
Modern writers group Simbi and Mami Wata as African-diasporic water spirits.

Manbo Ayizan.note: Sobo leaves Ayizan's household, establishes ritual flags and the laplas, then departs with Bade.

Marinette.note: Modern catalogues sometimes pair Marinette with Dantò in Petwo service, without recording a narrative encounter.

Marinette Bwa Chèch.note: Deren and Métraux describe Marinette as Ti Jean's wife or companion.
Marinette and Ti Jean are jointly invoked to light the fire.

Mary Magdalene.note: Modern summaries occasionally pair Brigitte with Mary Magdalene’s saint image.

Mawu.note: Scholars and practitioners comparatively equate both as supreme creators above active spirits.
At Mawu's request, Ayido-Hwedo coils beneath the overburdened earth to support it.
Divided-gender accounts enumerate Gu among Mawu's children.
Online sources occasionally assert Mawu as an African form of Brigitte.
Mawu is the female, lunar component or aspect of the compound creator.
Some traditions name Mawu alone as Legba’s mother.

Mawu.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
Mawu.note: Legba inspects the divine children’s kingdoms and reports to Mawu.

Mawu.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
Mawu.note: Mawu gives Legba knowledge of all divine languages.
Mawu judges Legba successful at playing instruments while dancing.
Mawu rewards Legba with Konikoni and precedence among the gods.

Minona.note: Mawu transmits divinatory knowledge through Minona, who teaches palm-kernel divination.

Monsieur Agoussou.note: Papa Lébat or Liba opens the ritual door to Monsieur Agoussou.

Monsieur Assonquer.note: Papa Lébat or Liba opens the ritual door to Monsieur Assonquer.

Moses.note: Serpent-bearing images of Moses provide another documented Catholic correspondence for Damballa.
Moses' serpent staff and bronze serpent support a localized identification with Danbala.

Mèt Kalfou.note: Bossou Koblamin is described as Kalfou's soldier or hired blade.
They hold complementary, variably paired authority over Rada and Petwo crossroads.

Naete.note: Mawu-Lisa produces Naete as one of the paired water deities.
Mawu-Lisa assigns Naete jurisdiction over the sea and waters.
Pantheon genealogies commonly list Naete among Legba’s siblings.

Naete.myth: Distribution of divine realms and languages
Naete.note: Legba connects Naete’s sea domain with Mawu through translation.

Naeté.note: Naeté is variously described as Agbé's sister or female twin.
Some African genealogies describe Naeté as Agbé's sister-wife or spouse.
Agbé and Naeté form a paired marine power inhabiting the sea.

Nana Buluku.myth: Nana Buluku produces the divine twins
Nana Buluku.note: Nana produces Mawu-Lisa and then withdraws or delegates cosmic rule.
Nana creates the universe and entrusts its government to Mawu-Lisa.

Nyohwe Ananu.note: She is regionally classified as mother of all Sakpata and of initiates.
One genealogy presents her as Da Zodji's twin within paired Sakpata.
One genealogy presents her as Da Zodji's spouse within paired Sakpata.

Ogou Ashade.note: Ogou Ashade belongs to the Ogou family and uses herbs to heal wounds.

Ogou Badagri.note: Ogou Badagri is a related Ogou with differentiated military and political roles.

Ogou Balendjo.note: Ogou Balendjo serves as captain of Agwe's ship Imamou in some accounts.
Ogou Balendjo belongs to the Ogou family and heals wounds.

Ogou Balenjo.note: Some Dominican and Haitian systems call Ti Jean Dantor his lieutenant.

Ogou Feray.note: Ogou Feray is classified as a militant, iron-working member of the Ogou family.

Our Lady of Częstochowa.note: Dantò is principally represented through the scarred dark Madonna and Child image associated with Częstochowa.

Our Lady of Mount Carmel.note: Some houses identify Dantò through Our Lady of Mount Carmel and observe her July feast.
Some regional practice associates Freda with this Marian figure, especially around Saut-d'Eau.

Our Lady of Prompt Succor.note: Some houses use Our Lady of Prompt Succor as Dantò’s Catholic visual correspondence.

Pandora.note: Modern comparativists analogize Pandora and Kalfou through the release of misfortune.

Rada lwa.note: Rada lwa are normally invoked earlier, with Petwo lwa attending later.

Sagbata.note: Sagbata and Agbé are siblings assigned the earth and sea.

Saint Andrew.note: Contemporary devotional and commercial sources sometimes identify Saint Andrew with Kalfou.

Saint Anne.note: Some houses pair Ayizan with Saint Anne through age, maternity, and ancestral female authority.

Saint Anthony of Padua.note: Modern Louisiana occult literature equates Monsieur Agassou with Saint Anthony.
Some Haitian and Dominican lineages locally associate this saint with Legba.

Saint Anthony the Abbot.note: Some Haitian and Dominican lineages locally associate this saint with Legba.

Saint Anthony the Great.note: De Heusch reports this Catholic correspondence, though the saint may also represent Simbi.

Saint Anthony the Hermit.note: Contemporary devotional and commercial sources sometimes identify Saint Anthony the Hermit with Kalfou.

Saint Barbara.note: Catholic inhabitants of Abomey associated Xevioso with Saint Barbara as protector against lightning.

Saint Brigid of Kildare.note: Later sources pair Brigitte with Saint Brigid; historical derivation remains unproved.

Saint Clare of Assisi.note: Ayizan is paired with Saint Clare through purity, whiteness, clarity, and female religious authority.

Saint Expedite.note: Contemporary devotional and commercial sources sometimes identify Saint Expedite with Kalfou.

Saint Expeditus.note: His image may represent Papa Gede or Bawon in some houses.

Saint George.note: Martial Ogou is regionally approached through Saint George's warrior iconography.
Some lineages pair the mounted dragon-slayer with Feray or another Ogou.
Saint George.source: Contemporary lineage testimony and pilgrimage reporting

Saint Gerard Majella.note: Gede imagery is regionally associated with this Catholic saint.
His chromolithograph may serve as Papa Gede’s visible image without implying full identity.

Saint Isidore the Laborer.note: Azaka is paired iconographically with the farmer saint through agriculture, blue clothing, and rural labor.

Saint James the Greater.note: Ogou is served through the mounted warrior saint and his feast.
Ogou inhabits or is served through Saint James’s mounted-warrior image.

Saint John the Baptist.note: Contemporary houses represent Ti Jean Dantor by the young saint and celebrate him June 24.

Saint Joseph.note: A practitioner website proposes Saint Joseph as a protective parallel.
Joseph's image and feast serve as Loko's Catholic counterpart in Haitian practice.

Saint Lazarus.note: Diasporic Catholic syncretism links the disease complex with Saint Lazarus.

Saint Lazarus the bishop.note: Modern devotional commerce sometimes confuses this saint with the beggar Lazarus.

Saint Martin de Porres.note: Popular references pair Baron or Baron Kriminel with this Catholic saint.
His image may represent Papa Gede or Bawon in some houses.

Saint Michael.note: A practitioner website proposes Saint Michael as a protective parallel.
Contemporary devotional and commercial sources sometimes identify Saint Michael with Kalfou.

Saint Nicholas.myth: Saint Nicholas and the three children
Saint Nicholas.note: Haitian interpretation casts the pictured children as Marassa and Nicholas as their rescuer and protector.

Saint Patrick.note: Catholic images of Patrick with serpents provide Damballa’s most frequent visual counterpart.
Haitian iconography represents Danbala through Saint Patrick because the saint's images include snakes.
Saint Patrick.source: Desmangles, The Faces of the Gods

Saint Paul.myth: Shared feast of Peter and Paul
Saint Paul.note: Bade is associated with Paul because Peter and Paul share the feast of 29 June.

Saint Peter.note: Keys and guardianship of heaven’s gate support their iconographic correspondence.
Sobo is equated with Peter through thunder-stones and the Gospel image of Peter as rock.

Saint Philip.note: Rigaud records Saint Philip as a correspondence for Ogou Feray.

Saint Raphael.note: Some houses associate Simbi with the healing and water-linked archangel Raphael.

Saint Roch.note: Rigaud reports a northern Haitian identification of Sobo with Saint Roch.

Saint Sebastian.note: Saint Sebastian’s tree-bound image serves as Gran Bwa’s Catholic visual counterpart.
Saint Sebastian.source: Vodou iconographic tables and practitioner accounts

Saint Ulrich.note: Agwe corresponds iconographically to Saint Ulrich through the fish in Ulrich's image.
Saint Ulrich.source: Métraux; Desmangles, Faces of the Gods

Saints Cosmas and Damian.note: Some Haitian systems use their paired image to represent Sobo and Badé.
The twin physician-martyrs provide the Marassa’s paired Catholic image and reinforce healing associations.
Late practitioner literature identifies the paired Sobo and Bade with Cosmas and Damian.

Santa Muerte.note: Neopagan writing joins Brigitte to Santa Muerte as a death-associated female power.

Segbo.note: Segbo is Hevioso’s father in the localized birth narrative.
Segbo tries repeatedly to destroy Hevioso, then attacks him and his mother.

Simbi Andezo.note: Invoked with Dlo and Makaya as the Three Simbis or Kings.

Simbi Dlo.note: Invoked with Andezo and Makaya as the Three Simbis or Kings.

Simbi Makaya.note: Modern queer and diasporic accounts sometimes identify Simbi Makaya as Dantò’s husband or partner.
Invoked with Dlo and Andezo as the Three Simbis or Kings.

Simityè.note: Kalfou and Simityè are both served by reported Makaya, Bizango, and Sanpwel groups.

St Philomena.note: Her local cult is intertwined with Lasyrenn despite ecclesiastical efforts at separation.

Tegbesu.myth: Bossou Ashadeh as the deified Dahomean king
Tegbesu.note: Bossou Ashadeh is identified as King Tegbesu transformed into a lwa after death.

Virgin Mary.note: Rigaud associates Ayizan's ritual purity with the Virgin Mary's virginity.
Marian sorrow imagery represents Freda's heart and tears without making the beings universally identical.
Maritime Marian imagery provides a possible modern analogy, but no universal equivalence.

Wututu.note: Later summaries identify the bird Wututu as Sogbo’s messenger.

Yemowo.note: Mawu is historically equated with Yemowo or Mowo in diffusion theories.

Yoruba Èṣù.note: Comparable messenger and crossroads powers encouraged scholarly comparison and partial Atlantic fusion.

every individual vodun.note: Each vodun may have a Legba acting as shrine guardian, executor, and right arm.

royal toxosu.myth: The royal toxosu origin of Bossou's three horns
royal toxosu.note: Bossou is explained as a royal anomalous child spirit whose bodily protrusions became horns.

the Virgin Mary.note: Mary intercedes before Bondye through Catholic prayer incorporated into Vodou practice.

the dead.note: Agwe may convey or shelter ancestral souls in the waters below.

the god of the whites.note: The just creator supporting the enslaved is morally opposed to the enslavers’ God.
the god of the whites.source: Dumesle, Voyage dans le nord d’Hayti

the lwa.myth: Creation and delegation of worldly domains
the lwa.note: Bondye creates or empowers the lwa and delegates worldly domains to them.
Some practitioners describe the lwa as Bondye’s servants, emissaries, or subordinate agents.
the lwa.source: Desmangles, The Faces of the Gods

the other Haitian lwa.note: Legba opens the gate through which the other lwa are saluted.

the other Ogous.note: Many houses describe the Ogous as brothers within one warrior family.
Some houses organize the distinct Ogous as fellow officers in a military company.

the saints.note: Saints intercede before Bondye and may serve as counterparts or faces of lwa.

Ázlì.note: Scholars propose a historical relationship, but the male Beninese vodun is not simply identical with Freda.

Èzili Dantò.note: Migrants invoked Agwe and Èzili Dantò before dolphins reportedly guided their boat ashore.
Late traditions describe Freda and Dantò as sisters, rivals, or complementary counterparts.
They fight over Ogou; some versions blame Freda for Dantò's scars or silencing.

Èzili Freda.note: Later sources variously call Èzili Freda Agwe's wife or mistress.

Èzili Freda.myth: Social and ritual contrast between Dantò and Freda
Èzili Freda.note: Dantò’s protective working motherhood contrasts with Freda’s luxury and frustrated romance.
They fight over a male spirit; varying versions explain Dantò’s wounds or Freda’s pierced heart.

Èzili Je Wouj.note: Some classifications identify Red-Eyes as Dantò’s enraged or hotter form; others consider her separate.
Where treated as a distinct lwa, Red-Eyes is classified as Dantò’s companion.

Ọbalúayé.note: Afro-Brazilian traditions identify this earth-disease power with Sakpata.
